awd_titl_txt: Conference: A Workshop to Train the Next Generation of Scholars at the Interface of AI, Environmental Gradients, and Infectious Disease Modeling
awd_abstract_narration:
The emergence of infectious diseases continues to pose significant global health challenges, exacerbated by environmental changes and increasing human mobility. Vector-borne diseases, such as malaria, dengue, and Lyme disease, are particularly sensitive to climatic and ecological shifts, which influence vector populations and disease transmission patterns. At the same time, advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have revolutionized the ability to analyze complex datasets and predict disease outbreaks with greater accuracy. Despite the growing importance of AI and environmental gradients in infectious disease research, there remains a substantial training gap in integrating these approaches into predictive modeling. This award supports a workshop at the 22nd annual Ecology and Evolution of Infectious Diseases conference to provide graduate students and postdoctoral researchers with hands-on training at the intersection of AI, environmental science, and infectious disease modeling. By equipping early-career scientists with these interdisciplinary tools, this initiative enhances the ability to develop adaptive surveillance systems, inform public health interventions, and mitigate emerging infectious disease threats in a changing world.

The workshop will offer an intensive two-and-a-half-day program featuring quantitative and applied training sessions. Participants will engage in parallel tracks, learning to apply Bayesian inference for estimating environmental response functions or utilizing AI techniques to analyze environmentally driven infectious disease patterns. Instructors with expertise in quantitative disease ecology and machine learning will guide trainees through hands-on exercises and collaborative group projects, reinforcing the application of these tools to real-world epidemiological challenges. The workshop’s structure ensures that participants develop both technical proficiency and an understanding of how to translate their research into actionable insights. To maximize accessibility, all instructional materials, including recorded sessions and coding resources, will be made publicly available. This initiative not only advances scientific knowledge but also fosters collaboration within the infectious disease research community, helping to prepare the next generation of scientists to tackle global health challenges.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Emerging infectious diseases are increasingly influenced by environmental change, including climate variability, land-use change, and shifting ecological conditions. At the same time, advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and data science are creating new opportunities to understand, predict, and respond to disease threats. This project addressed a critical need to train the next generation of scientists to work at the intersection of AI, environmental science, and infectious disease research.

With support from the National Science Foundation, we organized and delivered a 2.5-day intensive workshop, held June 14–16, 2025, at the University of Notre Dame immediately before the annual Ecology and Evolution of Infectious Diseases (EEID) conference. The workshop brought together graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, and instructors from diverse institutions and backgrounds to learn modern quantitative approaches for studying how environmental conditions influence disease dynamics.

Participants received hands-on training in two complementary areas: artificial intelligence and machine learning methods, and Bayesian statistical approaches for modeling disease systems. Through practical coding exercises in Python and R, participants learned how to analyze complex datasets, identify environmental drivers of disease, and develop predictive models that can improve understanding of disease risk. Small-group projects allowed trainees to apply these methods to real-world problems and present their findings, strengthening both technical and communication skills.

The intellectual merit of this project lies in advancing the capacity of researchers to use emerging computational tools to address important scientific questions about infectious diseases. The workshop helped bridge the gap between rapidly evolving analytical methods and their application to environmental and disease ecology. By exposing participants to both established and cutting-edge approaches, the project strengthened the methodological foundation of a growing interdisciplinary field and encouraged innovative research at the interface of ecology, epidemiology, and data science.

The broader impacts of the project were substantial. The workshop helped develop a highly skilled workforce prepared to tackle complex public health and environmental challenges. Participants gained expertise that can be applied to understanding diseases such as malaria, dengue, and other environmentally sensitive infections, supporting future efforts in disease surveillance, forecasting, and intervention planning. The workshop also emphasized how quantitative tools can inform conservation, environmental management, and policy decisions.

A major focus of the project was expanding access to advanced training opportunities. Travel support and targeted recruitment helped bring together participants from a wide range of institutions, disciplines, and geographic regions, including international participants and individuals who may otherwise have had limited access to specialized computational training. By lowering barriers to participation, the project broadened engagement in data-intensive approaches to environmental and health research.

The project also generated lasting educational resources. Workshop lectures, coding tutorials, exercises, and project materials were organized for continued use and dissemination, enabling participants to revisit the content and allowing others in the broader scientific community to benefit from the training. These openly shared resources provide a foundation for future workshops, courses, and self-directed learning.

Overall, this project successfully demonstrated that intensive, interdisciplinary training can effectively prepare early-career researchers to use AI and quantitative modeling approaches to address pressing challenges at the intersection of environmental change and infectious disease. By strengthening scientific capacity, fostering collaboration, and expanding access to modern analytical tools, the project contributes to a more resilient and well-prepared scientific workforce capable of addressing emerging global health challenges.
